sourceTranslationNote: Gihr 1902 title page states TRANSLATED FROM THE SIXTH GERMAN EDITION. It is a historical English translation, not Gihr's German autograph. Corpus Thomisticum identifies the Latin as Leonine 1906 text, machine-transcribed and subsequently checked by Enrique Alarcón.
criticalDistinctions: Published Mass ritual remains governed by 1962 Missale Romanum, not allegorical comments by St Thomas or historical notes by Gihr.
Corpus Thomisticum is an accessible checked Latin digital transcription, not the printed Leonine page images.
Gihr's OCR confirms text proximity but is not scanned-page reading, textual edition collation or rights approval.
A named locus groups multiple claims but each author's exact meaning and page scope remains independently reviewable.

witnesses.textBase: Latin Leonine 1906, with Busa/Alarcón digital correction
1902 B. Herder English translation from sixth German edition

rows.contextDescription: Aquinas gives symbolic interpretations of successive signs of the Cross as a depiction of the Passion; not a reconstruction of the historically original ritual.
rows.additionalHold: Leonine printed-page facsimile and any English/French translation remain uncollated; distinguish this argument from normative 1962 rubrics.

rows.contextDescription: The post-consecration signs do not perform another consecration or blessing of Christ; they recall the power of the Cross and Passion.
rows.additionalHold: Leonine printed-page facsimile and any English/French translation remain uncollated; no claim about modern ritual rule.

rows.contextDescription: The OCR discusses consecration as the supreme blessing, multiple interpretations of adscripta, and prefers the sense approved in accordance with Christ's institution; ratam discussed at the page boundary.
rows.additionalHold: All exact words and page breaks require page-image collation; Pauline citation in the footnote concerns the blessed chalice and must not be assigned to each adjective.

rows.contextDescription: The sequence of five adjectives in Quam oblationem forms Gihr's exposition of the desired oblation and change of the gifts.
rows.additionalHold: Printed-page images and exact adjective-by-adjective scope remain to be collated.

rows.contextDescription: The term rationabilis is discussed as reasonable/spiritual oblation, with an explicit Romans 12:1 source given in Gihr's footnote.
rows.additionalHold: Distinguish author's theological interpretation and Pauline citation from word-for-word borrowing of the entire Roman Canon text.

rows.contextDescription: The pp. 660 treatment of Melchisedech's bread and wine as a typological figure of the Eucharistic Sacrifice is located.
rows.additionalHold: Earlier pp. 75–76 have not been separately checked; retain a partial flag. Do not convert typology into proof that the Canon existed in Genesis.

rows.contextDescription: Abel's offering, Hebrews 11:4, Abraham and Isaac are treated as accepted typological sacrifices; Gihr explicitly frames heavenly fire concerning Abel as conjectural.
rows.additionalHold: Fire from heaven is not stated in Genesis 4; the inference must remain author-attributed and not enter the Bible narrative.

rows.contextDescription: The Lamb of God terminology is connected with Christ and the Eucharistic Communion invitation invoking St John the Baptist.
rows.additionalHold: Do not infer that every variant of the ritual Communion invitation had identical historical wording; printed page remains uncollated.

rows.contextDescription: Gihr's note reviews older multiple miserere nobis usages and subsequent third dona nobis pacem, distinguishing the sequence historically.
rows.additionalHold: 1962 Requiem and Holy Week variants are governed by the Missal, not the older historical commentary.

rows.contextDescription: The Agnus Dei threefold petition and its evolution from repetitive mercy petitions to a concluding peace petition are discussed in Gihr's historical account.
rows.additionalHold: Historical account cannot overrule 1962 liturgical form conditions; printed-page images remain uncollated.
